findings.where: The full-bleed house-blue band straight after the hero ('Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' / Subscribe), on desktop and phone
findings.fault: A second call to action sits right under the first screen. It is the most saturated block on the page, with display type as large as the hero line, so it beats 'Write to me directly' in a squint and gives the page two competing actions. Subscribe points to #subscribe, but the parts map shows nothing on the page for it to land on, so it looks like a dead action. The band also drops into the third person ('Mark's briefings') after a first-person hero, and it promises a briefings service that the brief does not say exists.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose brief asks for one message and one quiet action, with Mark's own voice and no invented offers. A development-bank visitor who clicks Subscribe and nothing happens, and who reads a shift into marketing copy.

findings.where: Article specimen: the 'Streamlining the PPP Process' lecture card
findings.fault: The card has a download arrow and the label 'PDF', but the link goes to #article and not to a file, so it promises a download it doesn't give. It also stacks a blue tint, a blue border, rounded corners and a wide soft shadow on a resting element. Nothing else on the page has a radius or a shadow, so it looks like a promo widget rather than part of the page's flat, square language.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who wants the lecture slides and gets an in-page jump. The founder, because the research names the PDF list as 'the product', so this one entry has to work and has to look like it belongs.

findings.where: Article specimen: body paragraphs, the subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?' and the numbered list, on desktop and phone
findings.fault: All the running text is centred. Long paragraphs are ragged on both edges, and the list's wrapped lines are centred while their numbers hang at the left margin. Each item's text drifts away from its number, so the three items don't read as a list.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and Mark's readers. The article page is the 'Read' surface, and centred multi-line prose is slow to read and makes the list hard to follow. This is the specimen the brief says must show how the content will hold up.

findings.where: Hero photograph: the keyed cut-out of Mark, on desktop (right) and phone (above the line)
findings.fault: The keyed treatment cuts Mark out of his talk. The lectern and setting are gone, leaving a floating head-and-shoulders with a soft halo around the hair and a hard diagonal edge across the suit at bottom left. On phone the head floats above the heading and the shoulders are cut off by the type. 'Mark at work' reads as a pasted headshot sticker, not a full-bleed photograph of him speaking.
findings.who_objects: The founder: the v7 card asks for a full-bleed photograph of Mark speaking, real people in real light. A visitor who notices the cut edge reads it as amateur compositing.

findings.where: Hero nav bar (name and logo only)
findings.fault: The nav holds only 'Mark M. Moseley' (static) and the logo link home. There is no navigation (articles, about, contact), even though the palette lists 'nav links' as a use for mist on slate. A first-time visitor can't see what else the site holds.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader arriving from LinkedIn who wants his work or publications before writing. First-visit trust asks for a Contact label in the navigation, and the brief's first screen calls for a nav.

findings.where: Section labels below the fold: 'PALETTE' (blue tracked capitals), 'Type pair', 'An article page' and 'Motion sketch' (small bold sans), 'Texture' (large italic serif)
findings.fault: Labels of the same kind get three different treatments. 'PALETTE' also uses both things the page's own type note rules out: tracked capitals, and blue on text that isn't clickable (the note says 'blue only where something can be clicked'). 'Texture' looks like a heading of a different rank.
findings.who_objects: The founder, comparing tiles, who sees the style tile contradict its own rules. A reader, who is told blue means clickable and then meets a static blue label.
